summary: Defines a MIB extension to the GBOND-MIB module with objects for managing Ethernet-based multi-pair bonded DSL interfaces, as described in the ITU-T recommendation. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When phone wires are bundled and carry Ethernet data, this memo gives network managers a standard set of dials to watch and adjust the bundle.

subtitle: SNMP objects for managing bundles of DSL lines that carry Ethernet traffic as one logical link.

tldr.problem: ITU-T G.998.2 bonds multiple xDSL lines into one Ethernet link, but operators lacked standard SNMP objects for the Ethernet-specific parts such as encapsulation type and the optional Bonding Aggregation Control Protocol (BACP).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6767 defines the G9982-MIB module with two groups, g9982Port for port configuration, capabilities, status and performance monitoring, and g9982Bce for per-channel status and BACP configuration, used together with GBOND-MIB.
tldr.outcome: Operators can manage G.Bond/Ethernet ports over SNMP. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6767 is a Proposed Standard, published in February 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used together with the GBOND-MIB of RFC 6765.

sections.title: What G.Bond/Ethernet Is and What This MIB Covers
sections.content:
Ethernet-based xDSL multi-pair bonding, or G.Bond/Ethernet, is specified in ITU-T Recommendation G.998.2. It bonds (aggregates) multiple xDSL lines, or individual bearer channels in multiple xDSL lines, into a single bidirectional logical link carrying Ethernet traffic.

RFC 6767 defines the G9982-MIB module, which provides objects specific to G.Bond/Ethernet and extends the common bonding objects of the GBOND-MIB from RFC 6765. Like the rest of the family it is a Management Information Base module meant to be accessed through SNMP, written in SMIv2, and it builds on the Broadband Forum report TR-159, which defines a management model and object hierarchy for bonded xDSL interfaces.
sections.eli5: Several phone wires can be joined so they work like one big internet cable. This memo lists the settings and meters for managing that big cable.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
A G.Bond/Ethernet port is a special case of a bonded multi-pair xDSL interface, so it is managed with the generic objects of the IF-MIB from RFC 2863, and ifIndex indexes both ports and individual xDSL lines and channels. The GBOND-MIB of RFC 6765 covers what all bonded interfaces share, such as bonding management, port and channel configuration, handshake-based discovery and the initialization sequence. Both GBOND-MIB and G9982-MIB are REQUIRED to manage a G.Bond/Ethernet port.

The RFC also compares this work with the EFM Copper MIB (EFM-CU-MIB) from RFC 5066, which manages the 10PASS-TS and 2BASE-TL interfaces of IEEE 802.3. G.998.2 extends the IEEE 802.3 Clause 61 bonding to work over any xDSL technology, bonding individual channels as well as physical lines. It also allows alternative HDLC encapsulation instead of the default 64/65-octet encapsulation, and adds the optional BACP. GBOND-MIB and G9982-MIB cover only the bonding part and leave the individual xDSL lines to their own line MIB modules. The EFM-CU-MIB has no historical performance monitoring, while the GBOND-MIB, G9982-MIB and xDSL line MIB combination provides it for the bonded link and the individual lines.

The RFC also notes that the IEEE 802.3 working group chartered a task force that continues development of Ethernet-related MIB modules based on the initial IETF work.
sections.eli5: There are two different toolboxes that can manage the same kind of cable. This memo explains how they overlap and which tool does which job.

sections.title: BACP-Based Discovery
sections.content:
All G.998 protocols share discovery of the remote Bonding Channel Entity (BCE) using the G.994.1 handshake (G.hs). Amendment 2 to G.998.2 adds an alternative optional Bonding Aggregation Control Protocol (BACP) for in-service discovery, aggregation and pair management. The default G.hs-based protocol cannot be used while the link is up.

The RFC gives pseudocode for automatic BCE assignment on a central office device with several Generic Bonding Sub-layer (GBS) ports. For each GBS port with room for more channels that uses BACP, it reads the eligible group ID and remote group ID from a connected BCE. It then looks through the disconnected channels that could be connected, and adds each whose remote group ID matches, up to the bonding capacity, to the GBS port through the ifStackTable. The RFC stresses this is only an example. Fixed pre-assignment, manual assignment or another internal algorithm may be used instead.

An SNMP agent builds the ifCapStackTable and its inverse on device initialization, from the device's cross-connect capabilities. When BACP is used, the g9982BceConfEligibleGroupID object MUST be updated automatically whenever those tables change.
sections.eli5: The wires need to find out which other wires lead to the same house before they can team up. BACP lets them do that without stopping the traffic.

sections.title: Structure of the G9982-MIB Module
sections.content:
The module splits its main objects into two groups, structured as RFC 4181 recommends. g9982Port holds configuration, capability, status and performance monitoring objects for G.Bond/Ethernet ports. The remaining port-level objects for the GBS port are in GBOND-MIB. g9982Bce holds optional per-channel status information and BACP configuration. Other BCE objects live in the relevant xDSL line MIB modules and in GBOND-MIB.

The optional performance monitoring counters, thresholds and history buckets are like those of TR-159 and use the 64-bit textual conventions of RFC 3705. The agent SHOULD align each interval with a fifteen-minute boundary of the wall clock, and each one-day interval with the start of a day. Counters are reset only when the agent is reset or re-initialized, not when a GBS is re-initialized.

A table in the RFC maps TR-159 attributes to SNMP objects. Examples include the PTM-TC encapsulation type (g9982PortConfTcAdminType), BACP support (g9982PortCapBacpSupported) and receive counters for errors, small, large, bad and lost fragments. Some of the mapping is only partial: the g9982PortPm* objects have no dedicated TR-159 attributes but are defined identically to the gBondPortPm* objects of GBOND-MIB, so they map to the corresponding TR-159 group performance attributes.
sections.eli5: The settings are put in two boxes, one for the whole bundle and one for each single wire in it, so each dial is easy to find.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects can hurt if unprotected. Changing g9982PortConfTable parameters such as g9982PortConfTcAdminType can cause a complete service interruption if the remote end does not support the chosen PTM-TC encapsulation. Changing g9982BceConfTable parameters such as g9982BceConfEligibleGroupID can stop a non-bonded BCE from joining any bonding group, or falsely advertise bonding eligibility, for example between BCEs on different line cards when cross-card bonding is not supported.

Readable objects can be sensitive too, since together they reveal performance and configuration. For example, objects in g9982PortStatTable such as g9982PortStatTcOperType may aid in deciphering the G.Bond/ETH transmissions. GET and NOTIFY access should be controlled, and values possibly encrypted in transit.

Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features. Those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy through the User-based Security Model with AES, and MAY support the Transport Security Model with SSH or TLS/DTLS. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: If anyone could turn the dials, the bundle could stop working, and if anyone could read the meters they might learn how to snoop. So only trusted people should be let in.
